ta-l1d7q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 7. Having shown that the proper principle of divine generation is nature, not will, Lombard asks whether the power of begetting is common to Father and Son, first taken concretely and then abstractly ('whether the Father is able by nature to beget the Son, and whether this is a power that is in the Son'). Thomas maps the determination, the confirming likeness, the doubt raised by an Augustinian text and some others' reasoning, and Lombard's solution. He announces two inquiries, on the power of begetting in God and on its commonness. The first has three articles: whether there is a power to beget in God, whether it is absolute or relative, and how it compares with the power to create.
claims: The proper principle of divine generation is nature, not will.
The power of begetting may be common to Father and Son taken concretely or abstractly.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e131.summary: First objection against a power to beget in God. Whatever proceeds from a power, whether of agent or matter, is in potency before it is in act, and the Son's generation is eternal.
claims: What comes from a power is first in potency before in act.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e134.summary: Second objection. What belongs to a nature per se does not come from it through an intermediate power, as the soul gives being to the body immediately. Generation is per se a work of nature (Damascene), so it is not a work of power.
claims: What belongs to a nature per se proceeds without intermediate power.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e137.summary: Third objection. Every power is active or passive. There is no passive power in the Father, otherwise he would be mother rather than father. There is no active power either, since active power is the principle of change in another as other (the Philosopher) and requires matter to act on, while the Son's generation is not from matter.
claims: Active power is the principle of change in another and requires matter.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e141.summary: Sed contra from Augustine: if the Father could not beget a Son equal and coeternal with himself, he was powerless. So divine power extends to the Son's generation.
claims: Inability to beget an equal Son would be impotence.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e147.summary: Second sed contra. Every operation shows the power of the operator. The act of generation infinitely surpasses the production of creatures, which manifests omnipotence, so the Son's generation manifests divine power all the more, as its act.
claims: Operations manifest the power of their agent.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e150.summary: Thomas's determination. In creatures, things are produced either by natural power, in likeness of the producer's nature (a man begets a man), or by rational power, in likeness of a form existing in the mind (a house built by an artisan). God produces in both ways. Something proceeds from God in likeness of nature, receiving the whole nature, the same not only in species but in number; this is the Son's procession by generation. So in God there is a power to beget like a natural power. Something also proceeds from God in likeness of an idea in the divine mind and does not receive the divine nature; these are creatures. So the power of operating on creatures is like a rational power in God, and omnipotence is understood according to it. The divine person proceeding by the quasi-natural power is not counted among all things, so the power to beget is not contained under omnipotence.
claims: God has a power to beget, analogous to natural power, by which the Son receives the numerically same nature.
God's power to create is analogous to rational power, and omnipotence concerns it.
The power to beget does not fall under omnipotence.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e153.summary: Reply to the first objection. The principle holds when an act differs really from the power it comes from, which must then be in potency before act, in time or nature. In God essence, power, and operation are really identical and differ only conceptually. Alternatively, among the divine persons there is only an order of nature by which one is from another, not before another (Augustine), so no priority follows from the Son's being begotten by the Father's power.
claims: In God power and act are really identical, so no priority of potency follows.
Among the persons there is an order of origin without priority.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e156.summary: Reply to the second objection. Nature or essence relates to two things: to its possessor and to that of which it is the principle. Between essence and possessor no power intervenes for the essence's act in the possessor, which is being; the essence gives being directly, and this is a kind of first act. Another act also proceeds from the essence, belonging to the possessor as agent and to the essence as principle of acting: second act, or operation. Between essence and operation an intermediate power intervenes, really distinct in creatures and conceptually in God. Begetting is such an act, so in our mode of understanding nature is its principle only through a power.
claims: Esse is first act, given immediately by the essence; operation is second act, mediated by power.
In God power is only conceptually distinct from essence and operation.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e159.summary: Reply to the third objection. Divine power is in no way passive, nor even active in the strict sense, but 'superactive'. Its action is not by way of motion but by way of operation, which differs from motion as perfect from imperfect, and so it needs no matter to act on. Action with motion needs matter, since motion is the passage from potency to act. So creation need not be from matter, still less divine generation. Avicenna says the divine agent differs from the natural: the natural agent causes motion, the divine gives the whole of being, as the creator of the world.
claims: Divine power is superactive, acting by operation rather than motion, and requires no matter.
The divine agent gives the whole of being, whereas natural agents cause motion.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e171.summary: First argument that the power to beget is relative. If the distinct persons are removed in thought, every absolute predicate remains (goodness, wisdom), but the power to beget does not. Removing the persons removes generation, and removing generation removes the power to beget, since in God nothing is in potency that is not in act; otherwise God would be mutable.
claims: Absolute predicates remain when the persons are abstracted; the power to beget does not.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e174.summary: Second argument. Powers are distinguished by acts, and begetting in God is relative, since generation is the relative property itself.
claims: Powers take their character from their acts.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e177.summary: Third argument. Every proper operation of a thing comes from its proper form, as burning from fire's form. Begetting is the Father's proper operation, so its principle is his proper form, paternity, a relation. Since the principle of operation is power, the power to beget is relative.
claims: Proper operations proceed from proper forms, and the Father's proper form is paternity.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e181.summary: Sed contra. Whose the act is, his is the power (the Philosopher). Generation is an act of nature (Damascene), so the power to beget belongs to the nature, which is said absolutely.
claims: The power belongs to whatever the act belongs to.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e184.summary: Second sed contra. In every univocal generation the principle and terminus are the same (man begets man). The terminus of divine generation is the essence communicated (Dist. 5), so the essence is also the principle, and the power to beget is essential.
claims: In univocal generation principle and terminus are the same.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e187.summary: Thomas's determination. Some held that the power to beget is relative both on the side of the act and on the side of the power, since power implies a relation of principle. Thomas rejects this: power is relative not in its being but only in its expression (secundum dici), and it signifies what is the principle, not only the relation of principle. The principle of every divine operation is the essence, which acts as wisdom, as will, and so on. Likewise, since the property is really the essence, the essence as paternity is the principle of begetting, not as agent but as that by which one acts. The principle of generation is thus the essence under the aspect of relation, a kind of mean between essential and personal. As the power, which mediates between essence and operation, is rooted in the essence, it is absolute; as it is joined to the operation, it is relative.
claims: Power is relative only secundum dici, not secundum esse.
The power to beget is the divine essence as identical with paternity, the principle by which the Father begets.
The power to beget is absolute as rooted in the essence and relative as joined to the operation.
concepts: relativum secundum esse vs. secundum dici
essence under the aspect of relation

ta-l1d7q1-d1e190.summary: Reply to the first argument. When the persons are removed in thought, what is purely absolute remains, but the power to beget is not purely absolute and so does not remain.
claims: The power to beget is not purely absolute.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e193.summary: Reply to the second argument. Although powers are known through acts, they need not belong to the same genus as their acts, especially active powers. So although begetting is relative, the power to beget need not be, though it is true that 'being able to beget' is being able toward something, in the accusative sense.
claims: Active powers need not share the genus of their acts.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e196.summary: Reply to the third argument. A common nature operates in each according to its condition, as the sensitive soul has different operations in different animals and organs, because the common nature is determined and contracted by each one's properties. The divine nature is not contracted or determined by the properties of the supposits, yet in the Father it is the Father's property and in the Son the Son's. It is not contracted, because the property is not other than the essence and so does not come to it as a contracting disposition. It is not distinguished, because relation is distinguished not according to what it is (in which it is identical with the essence) but according to being toward another, which concerns and distinguishes the person. So in the Father the nature is a principle of operation according to the Father's property, and the same operation belongs both to the common nature and to the Father's proper form. Hence the power to beget is a mean between absolute and relative. Those who called it absolute 'as remote or undisposed power' meant this, though improperly, since the property disposes the supposit, not the essence.
claims: The divine nature is not contracted or determined by personal properties, yet is in each person as that person's property.
The same act of begetting belongs to the common nature and to the Father's proper form.
Personal properties dispose the supposit, not the essence.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e200.summary: The answers to the remaining (sed contra) arguments follow from what has been said.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e212.summary: First argument that 'power' is not said univocally of the power to beget and the power to create. Powers are distinguished by acts and acts by objects, and the Son and creatures share nothing univocally, so neither do generation and creation or their powers.
claims: Powers are distinguished by acts, acts by objects.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e215.summary: Second argument. The power to create is simply absolute, the power to beget somehow relative, and nothing is univocal across absolute and relative, which are different categories.
claims: Absolute and relative are not univocal.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e218.summary: Contrary argument. The power to beget is the divine essence (art. 2), and so is the power to create, since God is first agent and all his operation is through his essence. So both are one power.
claims: Both powers are the divine essence.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e222.summary: Supposing that 'power' is said of them by priority and posteriority, which is prior? It seems the power to create, since the common precedes the proper and the essential precedes the personal in our understanding, and the power to create is common to the three while the power to beget belongs to the Father.
claims: The common and essential are prior in understanding to the proper and personal.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e225.summary: Contrary argument. The order of powers follows the order of acts, and generation is prior to creation as the eternal to the temporal, so the power to beget is prior.
claims: Generation is prior to creation as eternal to temporal.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e228.summary: Thomas's determination. In our understanding, power is a mean between essence and operation. The powers to create and to beget, considered as rooted in the essence, are numerically one power, let alone univocally named. Considered as joined to their operations, 'power' is said of them not univocally but by priority and posteriority, and the power to beget is prior in understanding to the power to create, as generation is prior to creation.
claims: As rooted in the essence, the powers to beget and to create are numerically one.
As joined to their operations, they are related by priority and posteriority, with the power to beget prior.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e231.summary: Reply to the first argument: it concerns power as compared to its act.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e234.summary: Reply to the second argument: the power to beget is relative only on the side by which it is joined to its act.
claims: The power to beget is relative only as joined to its act.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e237.summary: Reply to the third argument: it concerns, conversely, power as it stands on the side of the essence.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e241.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. In God the common precedes the proper in understanding when the common is taken in itself. When it is taken with a reference to creatures, it is posterior in understanding to what is proper to a person, because of that added reference.
claims: The common is prior to the proper in God only when taken without reference to creatures.

ta-l1d7q1-d1e244.summary: Concedes the fifth argument, that the power to beget is prior.

ta-l1d7q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 7 introduces Lombard's question whether the power of begetting is common to Father and Son, concretely and abstractly, and announces inquiries into the power of begetting and its commonness.

ta-l1d7q1-Dd1e123.summary: Article 1 asks whether there is a power to beget in God. Thomas distinguishes production by natural power (likeness of nature) from production by rational power (likeness of an idea). The Son proceeds by a quasi-natural power, receiving numerically the same nature, while creatures proceed by a quasi-rational power. Omnipotence concerns the latter, so the power to beget does not fall under omnipotence. The replies explain that power and act are really identical in God, so no priority follows. Esse is first act, given immediately by the essence, while operation is second act, mediated by power. Divine power is superactive, acting by operation, not motion, and so needs no matter.
claims: There is a power to beget in God, analogous to natural power.
The power to beget does not fall under omnipotence, which concerns creatures.
Divine power is superactive and needs no matter.

ta-l1d7q1-Dd1e163.summary: Article 2 asks whether the power to beget is absolute or relative. Rejecting the view that it is relative in itself, Thomas holds that power is relative only in expression and signifies what is the principle. The power to beget is the divine essence as identical with paternity, the principle by which the Father begets. It is absolute as rooted in the essence and relative as joined to the act, a mean between essential and personal. The divine nature is not contracted or determined by the personal properties, yet the same act of begetting belongs to the common nature and to the Father's proper form.
claims: The power to beget is the essence under the aspect of paternity, a mean between absolute and relative.
The divine nature is not contracted by personal properties.

ta-l1d7q1-Dd1e204.summary: Article 3 compares the power to beget with the power to create. As rooted in the essence they are numerically one power. As joined to their operations they are named by priority and posteriority, and the power to beget is prior, as eternal generation is prior to creation. The common is prior to the proper only when taken without reference to creatures.
claims: The powers to beget and to create are one as rooted in the essence.
As joined to their acts, the power to beget is prior to the power to create.

ta-l1d7q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 7 treats the power of begetting in God. Article 1 affirms such a power, modelled on natural power, by which the Son receives numerically the Father's nature. It contrasts this with the quasi-rational power by which creatures proceed according to ideas, to which alone omnipotence refers. Divine power is superactive, acting by operation rather than motion. Article 2 holds that the power to beget is the essence considered as identical with paternity: absolute as rooted in the essence, relative as joined to its act, a mean between essential and personal. Personal properties do not contract the common nature. Article 3 holds that the powers to beget and create are numerically one in the essence, but as joined to their acts the power to beget is prior, as generation is prior to creation.
claims: There is a power to beget in God, modelled on natural power and not falling under omnipotence.
The power to beget is the essence under the aspect of paternity, a mean between absolute and relative.
The powers to beget and create are one in the essence; the power to beget is prior as joined to its act.
